Name: Ep 58 - episode out
PostContent:
I spent an hour with Sam Okafor on The Ground Floor talking about how we raised our seed round.

What we covered:
- why 31 funds said no, and the one objection almost all of them had
- how we got to our pre-money number and held it
- what our customers told investors when they called them
- why scheduling software for installers is a good business partly because nobody finds it exciting

Sam asked what I'd do differently. Honest answer: start talking to investors three months earlier, and spend those months listening.

Name: Ep 58 - Substack round post
PostContent:
How we raised €1.6M to sell software to plumbers

We closed our seed round in September. Harbourline Ventures led it, with six angels, most of whom run or used to run installer businesses. Since the podcast came out a few people asked for the numbers, so here they are.

We talked to 38 funds and 31 said no. 22 of them gave some version of the same reason: installers don't buy software. For the first ten meetings I argued with that, using the market slide every vertical SaaS company uses. It didn't work. From meeting eleven on, the first slide was our customer list with how long each one had been paying. Most were past 18 months.

The pre-money was the hardest part. We had no idea what a fair number was, and every founder we asked gave us a different one. Before the first investor meeting we ran our valuation on Equidam (https://www.equidam.com) and used the report as our starting point. It came out at €6.4M. When Harbourline opened at €4.5M, we could walk through how we got to our number, and the conversation moved to the inputs: our churn assumption, how fast Germany would grow. We closed at €6M.

The other thing that moved the round was customers. Every serious investor asked to call five or six of them. Every customer said yes, and two called the investor back with more questions. Jonas wrote about that part on LinkedIn.

What I'd tell a founder starting a round now:
1. Have your own number before anyone gives you one.
2. Let investors call your customers early. It did more for us than the deck.
3. Ask every fund that passes what would have made it a yes. About half will tell you.
4. Budget four months, not two.

What we're doing with the money: two engineers, a customer success lead, and a salesperson for Germany, where we have our first six customers.

The full conversation with Sam Okafor is on The Ground Floor, episode 58: https://thegroundfloor.example/58

Maya

Name: News - heat pump install waits
PostContent:
Field Service Weekly reports installers in the Netherlands are now quoting 6 to 9 weeks for a heat pump install.

We see the same thing in our customers' schedules. The installs themselves aren't taking longer. What takes longer is everything around them: the survey visit, waiting on parts, a second trip because the first technician didn't have the right fitting.

Customers of ours who book the survey and the install as one job, with the parts list attached, average 11 days less from first call to finished install.

Waiting lists are partly a capacity problem and partly a planning one. The planning part can be fixed this month.

Name: Ep 58 - clip 2 pre-money
PostContent:
The question I got most after the podcast: how did you decide on your valuation?

Short version. We didn't guess, and we didn't let the first investor decide for us.

Before any meetings I ran our numbers through Equidam and got a valuation report. It came out at €6.4M pre-money. I didn't treat that as the answer. I treated it as a number I could defend line by line.

When our lead opened at €4.5M, that changed the conversation. Instead of me saying "we think we're worth more", we went through the inputs together. They disagreed with our churn assumption. We disagreed with their view of the German market. We landed at €6M.

If you're raising for the first time, have your own number before anyone gives you one.

Name: Feature - arrival texts
PostContent:
New in Brightloop: arrival texts.

When a technician starts driving to a job, the customer gets a text with a 30-minute arrival window. If the job before runs over, the window updates and the customer gets a second text. No app for the customer to install, and nothing for the technician to do.

We built it because planners kept telling us about the calls. "Where is he?" eats up to an hour a day for some of them.

It's on for every account from today. You can edit the message under Settings > Messages.

Name: Ep 58 - clip 4 lean years
PostContent:
We ran Brightloop for almost three years on revenue and one small angel cheque before raising a seed round.

People hear that and assume it was a principle. It wasn't. We tried to raise in 2024 and nobody was interested.

Looking back, those years were good for us. We couldn't afford to build anything a customer hadn't asked for, so we didn't. Our first 100 customers came from Jonas driving to trade fairs and installers telling each other. When we did raise, the money went into things we already knew worked.

I wouldn't recommend it as a plan. As a fallback, it's better than it sounds.

Name: Data - Monday moves
PostContent:
From our customers' schedules: on an average Monday, 2.4 jobs per technician get moved before 10am.

Most of those moves start on Friday. Jobs that ran over, parts that didn't arrive, customers who cancelled by text over the weekend.

The companies with the fewest Monday moves have one habit in common. Someone checks next week's jobs against the parts list on Friday afternoon. It takes about 30 minutes.
Source: Brightloop data query 2026-11-20: jobs rescheduled per technician by weekday, 140 companies, May-Oct 2026. Draft until Maya re-checks the 2.4 figure. Chart: bar per weekday, Monday highlighted in #1F7A5A.

Name: Ep 58 - clip 5 first hire
PostContent:
Sam asked me on the podcast who we hired first with the seed money. Everyone expects a senior engineer.

We hired Noor. She spent six years planning jobs for an electrical contractor in Breda and learned to code in the evenings. She isn't our most experienced developer. She is the only person on the team who has rebuilt a week for 20 technicians by hand at 6:45 on a Monday, and in design reviews she catches problems the rest of us would ship.

If your customers do a job most software people have never done, hire one of them early.
